name: RE/flex
workload: Tokenizing a 2 KB representative C source file into 244 tokens; elapsed time in microseconds, averaged over 1000-10000 benchmark runs, comparing reflex-generated scanners against Flex, Boost.Spirit.Lex, PCRE2 (JIT/DFA), Hyperscan, RE2, GNU POSIX regex, and std::regex (std::cregex_iterator).
claimed_speedup: 8.7-20.6 microseconds (RE/flex) vs 6490 microseconds for std::cregex_iterator() (std::regex) -- roughly 315x-746x faster on this tokenizing workload; also faster than PCRE2 JIT (500-60.8us) and Boost.Regex POSIX (205-392us) in the same table.
hardware: 2.9 GHz Intel Core i7, 16 GB 2133 MHz LPDDR3, Mac OS X 12.6.9
stars_or_usage: 599 stars; used by ugrep and the Tiger Compiler
tradeoffs: RE/flex is a Flex-style lexical-analyzer generator (requires a code-generation step to build a DFA-based scanner), not a drop-in std::regex object; PCRE2/Boost.Regex are optionally integrated for Perl-style matching, otherwise matching is DFA-based and linear-time; larger API/build surface than std::regex.
caveats: Benchmark table states compiler, flags, and hardware directly in the README (in-repo), but the downloadable test harness ('Download the tests') is hosted externally on genivia.com rather than committed to the git repo, so full independent reproduction requires that external zip. This is the author's own benchmark, not an independent third party.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'regex library faster than std::regex benchmark C++ 2026' -> github.com/Genivia/RE-flex

name: Boost.Regex
workload: 18 regex patterns (literal search, alternation such as 'Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn', character classes, bounded repeats, case-insensitive variants, one catastrophic-backtracking pattern) applied to a text corpus via the regex_perf tool, best time of 5 runs per pattern.
claimed_speedup: Roughly 1.8x-48x faster than libstdc++ std::regex across most of the 18 test patterns (e.g. 'Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn': 12.2 vs 591.3 units, ~48x; literal 'Twain': 8.7 vs 223, ~26x; '\u221e|\u221a': 7.3 vs 340.7, ~47x). One alternation pattern ran slower for Boost (800.8 vs 595). On a catastrophic-backtracking pattern std::regex took 17989 units while Boost was not measured (n/a).
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build, -O3, C++11 (built via default Ubuntu cmake/g++ toolchain; exact GCC version not printed in the README)
hardware: AMD Threadripper 3960X (Zen2) at 3.8 GHz, Ubuntu 20.04.5 LTS
stars_or_usage: 119 stars on this GitHub submodule mirror (boostorg/regex); Boost overall is one of the most widely deployed C++ library collections
tradeoffs: Same backtracking-NFA design as std::regex (shares its ReDoS risk class); not header-only, requires linking the compiled Boost.Regex library; larger dependency footprint than std::regex.
caveats: Primary source's numbers are presented only as a PNG chart in the repo (results_20221012.png), not as a text/CSV table in the README; I opened and read the image directly. Exact GCC version is not printed. Cross-checked against two independent, weaker sources with matching direction: c0rp3n/regex-bench (std::regex 44.66ms vs boost::regex 4.88ms, ~9.2x, on an AMD Ryzen 2700X, compiler/flags unstated, archived 2-star repo) and mariomka/regex-benchmark (C++ Boost 104ms vs C++ STL 1021ms total, ~9.8x, g++ -std=c++11 -O3, macOS Core i9, 334-star repo). GitHub's license auto-detector reports 'null' for this submodule repo, but Boost.Regex ships under the standard Boost Software License 1.0 as part of the Boost distribution.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'C++ regex engine benchmark shootout PCRE2 RE2 std::regex boost speed comparison' -> rust-leipzig/regex-performance; cross-checked via WebSearch 'regex library faster than std::regex benchmark C++ 2026' -> c0rp3n/regex-bench, mariomka/regex-benchmark

name: REAL (real-regex)
workload: 12 general-purpose regex patterns (word/digit/field extraction, single-char class, bounded repeats, possessive quantifiers, alternation, date/hex matching, literal, anchored, lookahead) scanning the same corpus and counting non-overlapping matches, in nanoseconds per corpus byte; median of 30 paired batches x 3 runs (minimum taken per cell), match counts verified equal across engines on the same commit.
claimed_speedup: 8.20x-41.97x faster than std::regex (libstdc++) on x86-64 (g++ 13.3.0); 15.31x-151.97x faster than std::regex (libc++) on arm64 (Apple clang 16). Also faster than RE2 in every case it supports (2.90x-16.34x on x86-64, 2.41x-11.53x on arm64) and beats PCRE2-JIT on 7 of 12 patterns on both ISAs.
compiler_and_flags: c++ -std=c++20 -O2 (per benchmarks/Makefile 'bench-engines' target); g++ 13.3.0 on x86-64, Apple clang 16 on arm64
hardware: x86-64 host (exact CPU model not named in the doc) and arm64 Apple Silicon (measured on AC power, per the project's own measurement-methodology notes)
stars_or_usage: 4 stars; very new project (repo created June 2026)
tradeoffs: Requires C++20 (std::regex only needs C++11); rejects backreferences and conditional groups by design to keep linear-time guarantees, so it is not a full drop-in for all std::regex/PCRE patterns; PCRE2-JIT still wins on lookahead-heavy and some fixed-width date/hex patterns via backtracking; the multi-pattern (regex_set) N-walk mode degrades hard as pattern count N grows and loses to RE2::Set/Hyperscan at scale, per the project's own docs.
caveats: Extremely new, very small project (4 stars, created about 3 months before this evaluation) with essentially no external validation beyond its own test/benchmark suite. Its own BENCHMARKS.md is unusually self-critical, documenting past discrepancies ('drift') between prose summary bullets and the underlying measured tables, and explicitly cautions that absolute figures are noisy and hardware-dependent and should be treated as informational rather than a guarantee. Exact x86-64 CPU model is not named.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github C++ regex library drop-in std::regex replacement performance header-only' -> RECHE23/real-regex README -> docs/BENCHMARKS.md

name: Unformat
workload: Parsing the string 'Harry is 18 years old.' against the format '{} is {} years old.' to extract a string_view and an int, timed with Google Benchmark (single call latency, unformat_benchmark.cpp).
claimed_speedup: Unformat: 32.6 ns (11.5 ns using the compile-time constexpr make_format path) vs std::regex (StdRegex in the benchmark): 3269 ns -- roughly 100x-284x faster; the project's own description claims 'up to 300x faster than std::regex'.
hardware: 32 x 2420 MHz CPUs (exact CPU model and OS not stated)
tradeoffs: Not a general regex engine -- only handles fixed brace-delimited '{}' format-string extraction of basic types (similar to a type-safe scanf), with no wildcards, character classes, alternation, or quantifiers, so it cannot replace std::regex for general pattern matching; the win mainly reflects avoiding std::regex's NFA-compilation/allocation overhead for a task regex is overkill for.
caveats: Benchmark code (unformat_benchmark.cpp) is in-repo and buildable via CMake with Google Benchmark, but the README does not state compiler, optimization flags, or OS (only core count and clock speed) -- per the hard rule that unstated flags cap the tier, this is capped at C despite having reproducible in-repo code. Also, the workload being measured (typed parsing of one fixed format string) is a narrower task than general regex matching, so the comparison is not fully apples-to-apples with std::regex's broader feature set.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos 'regex faster than std::regex' (seed-query variant) -> adamyaxley/Unformat
